paragraphs.text: Form No. HCJD/C-121. ORDER SHEET IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT. Criminal Revision No.65936 of 2021. Firdous Akhtar Versus. Azmat Bashir Khokhar, etc. S.No. Of order/ Proceeding Date of order/ Proceeding Order with signature of judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary, 12.10.2026. Mr. Tanvir Ahmad Butt, Advocate for the petitioner Mr. Hamid Iftikhar Syed, DDPP for state. Mr. Faisal Rafique, Advocate for the respondents. Firdous Akhtar (petitioner), through instant Criminal Revision, has called into question the legality and propriety of the order dated 05.07.2017 passed by the learned Civil Judge, Lahore, whereby her application under Section 476, of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1898 (“Cr.P.C”), read with Section 195, Cr.P.C., and Section 193 of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (“PPC”), seeking initiation of criminal proceedings against respondents on the allegations of forgery, fabrication of documents and giving false evidence in judicial proceedings, was declined and upheld by learned Additional Sessions Judge vide order dated 23.06.2021.

Briefly stated, the controversy emanates from civil litigation between the parties, including a suit for specific performance instituted under the title “Waris Ali Chaudhry v. Mst. Firdous Akhtar and others”, wherein certain documents, including Exh.P-1, Exh.P-6, Exh.P-7 and Exh.P-8, were produced during the proceedings. The petitioner alleged that the said documents were forged, fabricated and self-engineered and that respondents had relied upon them to mislead the learned Civil Court. She consequently sought initiation of criminal proceedings against the persons allegedly responsible for preparing and using the disputed documents and for giving false evidence. The learned Civil Judge, vide order dated 05.07.2017, declined the requested relief by observing that judgment and decree passed in main civil suit on 11.03.2016 did not contain any finding regarding the alleged forgery or fabrication of documents in question. The application was dismissed as not maintainable in the circumstances of the case. Learned appellate Court, through judgment and decree dated 23.06.2021, also rejected the appeal and maintained decision. The petitioner seeks to pursue criminal proceedings on the basis of allegations which, according to her, were not properly examined during civil litigation.

Learned counsel for petitioner contends that respondents deliberately produced fabricated documents and tendered false evidence to secure an order in their favor. It is argued that learned lower Courts failed to examine the allegations despite the petitioner's application and that the disputed documents were instrumental in the judicial proceedings. Learned counsel maintains that the impugned order has been passed without proper appreciation of material available on record and, therefore, calls for interference by this Court.

Conversely, learned counsel for respondents supports impugned order and submits that petitioner is attempting to convert a civil dispute into criminal litigation. It is argued that neither the judgment of main suit nor appellate judgment records any finding establishing forgery or perjury. The respondents further maintain that mere production of documents during judicial proceedings, followed by an adverse decision in the civil litigation, does not furnish sufficient ground for initiating any criminal prosecution in absence of any findings.
Arguments advanced both pro and contra have been heard, and the record has also been examined.

The controversy requiring determination is whether material brought on record justifies initiation of proceedings under Section 476, Cr.P.C., read with Section 195, Cr.P.C., or whether the learned lower Courts committed illegality, material irregularity or jurisdictional defect by declining to attend petitioner's grievance. At the outset, it is appropriate to observe that the power to initiate a complaint in respect of offences allegedly committed in or in relation to judicial proceedings is not to be exercised mechanically. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Ch. Feroz Din’s case1 has placed a check upon the initiation of the proceedings holding that prosecution for perjury is to be directed only where it serves the interest of justice and not to satisfy private vengeance. This principle has since been reaffirmed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Qazi Naveed ul Islam’s case 2, wherein it was held that the power under section 476, Cr.P.C. is discretionary, as evident from the expression “may take cognizance”, and is to be exercised “judiciously, not arbitrarily”; that, notwithstanding the omission of the expression “it is expedient in the interests of justice” by Act XXI of 1976, the Court “should give prime consideration to the question, whether it is expedient in the interests of justice to take cognizance of the offence”; and that the Court “must be watchful of the fact that its process under section 476 is not abused by an unscrupulous litigant scheming to wreak private vengeance or satisfy a private grudge against a person.” The object of relevant statutory provisions is to protect the administration of justice from offences which tend to obstruct or pervert the course of judicial proceedings; therefore, the Court concerned must, therefore, examine the available material, the nature of alleged offence and necessity of prosecution in the interest of justice. The expediency contemplated by the law is to be gauged with reference to the administration of justice and not the private grievance of a litigant. The Hon’ble Supreme Court Pakistan in Ameer Rehman’s case 3 has emphasized that “perjury and fabrication of documentary evidence are to be taken very seriously by Courts”, the object being the protection of the administration of justice; it follows that where no such impact is shown, the jurisdiction is not to be set in motion. 1 Ch. Feroze Din v. DR. K. M. Munir and another (1970 SCMR 10) 2 Qazi Naveed ul Islam v. District Judge, Gujrat and others (PLD 2023 SC 298) 3 Ameer Rehman and others v. Ameer Mumtaz and others (2015 SCMR 1373) A Full Bench of this Court4 explained that the offences enumerated in section 195, Cr.P.C. “have been selected for the Court’s control because of their direct impact on the judicial process”, and that “As the purity of the proceedings of the Court is directly sullied by the crime, the Court is considered to be the only party entitled to consider the desirability of complaining against the guilty party.” The Full Bench further held (para 27) that “the proper place for the determination of a person’s guilt or innocence is a criminal and not a Civil Court or Revenue Court”, and that section 195, Cr.P.C., being a provision, which deprives the ordinary Criminal Courts of their ordinary jurisdiction, is to be construed strictly. The mere assertion that a document is forged or that a witness has given false evidence does not, by itself, make the initiation of criminal proceedings obligatory.

In present case, petitioner has primarily relied upon the documents produced in a civil litigation and alleged that same were forged or fabricated. However, the perusal of available record does not disclose any findings recorded by learned trial Court in its judgment dated 11.03.2016 establishing that Exh.P-1, Exh.P-6, Exh.P-7 or Exh.P-8 were either forged or prepared fraudulently. Likewise, subsequent appellate judgment dated 23.06.2021 does not record a determination holding the respondents guilty of committing forgery or perjury. The present petitioner has not been able to demonstrate from any material that learned Civil Judge or Appellate Court ignored to assess. The Court exercising jurisdiction under Section 476, Cr.P.C., must first satisfy, upon independent assessment of material brought, and then to assess the statutory requirements, whether same are fulfilled before initiating any proceeding upon a complaint, or whether it is expedient in the interest of justice to proceed in the matter. This Court observes that allegations made by petitioner have not been supported by any material sufficient to demonstrate that learned Civil Judge's refusal 4 in Muhammad Shafi v. Deputy Superintendent of Police (Malik Gul Nawaz), Narowal and 5 others (PLD 1992 Lahore 178, para 20) to initiate proceedings was arbitrary, capricious or contrary to law or the findings upheld by learned Appellate Court are illegal.

Petitioner's case is that disputed documents were produced during civil proceedings are fabricated, hence, should have been examined by the learned trial Court in that spirit. On perusal of record, it does not establish that production of documents was ever challenged by petitioner under objection or there finds mention sufficient finding on fact, holding them to be forged, and same from record does reveal determination which learned Civil Court wrongly held that respondents deliberately tendered false evidence with intent to deceive the Court. In the circumstances, petitioner's allegations for initiating any proceeding under the relevant provisions of law as allegations raised by petitioner are closely connected with the merits of civil controversy between the parties where from record it shows that dispute which formed part of background of civil litigation, culminated in a judgment and decree dated 11.03.2016, followed by Appellate proceedings, wherein nothing finds mention that the same were result of committing forgery with the Court in order to prove decision in their favor. Petitioner, thus, cannot seek for initiation of criminal prosecution merely by reiterating allegations which, according to her, were not adequately discussed in the civil judgment. What is required is material indicating that the alleged conduct constitutes an offence within the contemplation of law and that prosecution would serve a legitimate purpose in the administration of justice.

This Court also finds that petitioner's allegation that respondents acted in concert to prepare and rely upon those documents, particularly through special attorney who appeared in civil proceedings and produced the documents in question. However, mere fact that a person appeared as a special attorney and produced documents on behalf of a party does not, without supporting material, establish his involvement in forgery or perjury. Criminal liability cannot be inferred solely from the production of a disputed document, nor can a person be subjected to prosecution merely because he represented a party in civil litigation. In Muhammad Shafi’s case (supra, paras 23 and 27) held that clause (c) of section 195(1), Cr.P.C. applies only to those offences that have a “close nexus between the offence and the proceeding”, and “does not apply to cases in which the forgery was committed before the institution of a suit or other proceedings in which the forged document is produced or given in evidence”. Insofar as petitioner’s grievance relates to documents allegedly forged prior to their production in the civil suit, the proceedings under section 476, Cr.P.C. are not the appropriate forum, and the petitioner is not left without remedy under the general law. In these circumstances, petitioner's attempt to secure the initiation of criminal proceedings, without demonstrating the requisite material or the expediency of such action in the interest of justice, cannot be accepted merely on the strength of her bald assertions. The jurisdiction conferred by Section 476, Cr.P.C. read with Section 195, Cr.P.C., is intended to safeguard the purity of judicial proceedings5 and not to provide a forum for the pursuit of private vengeance6.The question before this Court is whether the statutory jurisdiction was properly invoked and whether impugned order suffers from any legal defect does not warrant interference by this Court; for the reasons discussed above, no such defect has been established.

In view of the foregoing discussion, this Court finds no sufficient ground to interfere with the impugned order dated 05.07.2017. Petitioner, thus, failed to demonstrate any illegality, material irregularity, or jurisdictional defect in the exercise of discretion by the Courts below. Concurrent conclusions of the Courts below can only be disturbed in revisional jurisdiction if the reasoning on which they rest is shown to be legally flawed. No such flaw has either been shown or found from the record of the 5 (Muhammad Shafi’s Case (Supra, para 20) 6 Ch. Feroz Din v. Dr. K.M. Munir, 1970 SCMR 10, and Qazi Naveed ul Islam v. District Judge, Gujrat and others, PLD 2023 SC 298. Both the cases have been referred to above in this judgment) proceedings. Consequently, the instant criminal revision is dismissed. (Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz) JUDGE Umar Hayat* APPROVED FOR REPORTING (Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz) Judge Blue Slip Add
